endorsements.title: Using ambient AI in clinical consultations: reframing policy around clinical audit and patient safety
endorsements.quote: Specific safeguards are needed for minors, for patients with low literacy, and for multilingual encounters, where the information supporting consent must itself be intelligible; in emergencies, where valid consent is impracticable, recording should default to off.

evidence.title: Acceptance of AI scribes within hospital allied health settings: A mixed methods study
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported contexts where AI scribe use may harm patient care, engagement or be contraindicated
evidence.effect: Clinicians reported AI scribe use needs careful consideration in certain contexts and may be contraindicated for patients with persecutory delusions involving surveillance (qualitative).
evidence.quote: They also highlighted that, in certain contexts, the use of AI scribes requires careful consideration to ensure patient care and engagement are maintained and that use with some patients (i.e., those experiencing persecutory delusions involving surveillance) may be contraindicated.
evidence.sample_unit: clinician survey responses (plus 27 clinician interviews, 19 patient surveys, 4 patient interviews)

evidence.title: Acceptability of AI-Assisted Psychotherapy to Prospective Patients and Their Intent to Continue Treatment: A Vignette Study
evidence.effect: Therapist AI use reduced acceptability and continuation intent versus control; all p<0.001; covert use produced strongest declines.
evidence.quote: Across all models, therapist use of AI substantially reduced perceived acceptability and continuation intent compared with the control scenario (all p<0.001).

commentary.bottom_line: No study tests whether turning AI off by default in sensitive encounter types, with documented case-by-case enablement, protects privacy, trust, or candor. Two hazard studies suggest that AI use in some mental health and surveillance-sensitive contexts may lower patient acceptance or be contraindicated, but neither evaluates the proposed safeguard.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two included studies document the hazard only. One is a descriptive survey and interview study, and the other is a vignette experiment with prospective patients. Neither compares default-off settings with any alternative, and the endorsing framework quote concerns change-of-control notice rather than sensitive encounters.

In an Australian deployment, clinicians reported that AI scribe use may be contraindicated for patients with persecutory delusions involving surveillance. This suggests a failure mode in which recording itself may worsen symptoms or disengagement. The study does not show whether a default-off rule would catch these cases before recording begins.

Among 201 United States adults reading therapy vignettes, therapist AI use reduced acceptability and intent to continue care compared with control (all p<0.001), and covert use produced the largest declines. These results suggest that patients may value knowing about and agreeing to AI use in sensitive care, though the setting was simulated.

The endorsing commentary calls for specific safeguards for minors, patients with low literacy, and multilingual encounters, and for recording to default to off in emergencies. The hazard studies do not report results for limited English proficiency, low-literacy, Medicaid, or safety-net patients, so the need these groups face under this practice remains untested.

commentary.research_gap: Pragmatic studies are needed that compare default-off with documented enablement against default-on with opt-out in encounter types such as mental health, reproductive care, substance use, care of minors, and emergencies. Useful outcomes would include patient disclosure and trust, continuation of care, clinician documentation burden, and how faithfully enablement decisions are recorded. Samples should include patients with limited English proficiency and low literacy.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study reports inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The commentary identifies low-literacy and multilingual encounters as needing added safeguards, but no data show how default-off rules or case-by-case enablement would work for these patients, so any benefit to them is unknown.
